d.title: Read the question, then pick the traversal
d.caption: **One question decides it: what is the answer shaped like?** If it is a distance, BFS reaches the nearest node first and you stop on discovery. If it is a path or a cycle, DFS is the only one whose call stack already holds the answer. **And the row people get wrong in interviews: BFS on a weighted graph gives the fewest edges, not the shortest distance** — swap the queue for a min-heap and the same template becomes Dijkstra.

d.title: The same six growth rates, counted out at three input sizes
d.caption: **This table is the reason complexity is taught before anything else.** At n = 10 every row is instant and the distinction looks academic. At a million, O(n log n) is still a fraction of a second and O(n squared) is a million million steps — **hours of work for the same answer.** The last row is the one to remember by shape rather than by number: **O(2^n) at n = 1,000,000 is not slow, it is impossible**, and no faster machine changes that.

d.title: Choose, explore, un-choose - and the prune that does the work
d.caption: **Every backtracking solution you will ever write is this loop.** The un-choose step is what makes it cheap: one set of sets serves every branch, because each branch tidies up after itself. And the prune is where the saving lives — **8-Queens by brute force is 16,777,216 boards, while abandoning a branch the moment two queens attack finds all 92 solutions in about two milliseconds.** Same search space, one check added.
